evidenceAudit.scope: Head injury and traumatic brain injury in adults and children in India from prehospital care to discharge: Glasgow Coma Scale (GCS) grading, airway, breathing and circulation, computed tomography (CT) indications, admission and surgical criteria, raised intracranial pressure (ICP) treatment, seizure prophylaxis and discharge, built on the ICMR Neurosurgery STW for Head Injury (July 2024).
findings: GCS bands (13–15 mild, 9–12 moderate, 3–8 severe), CT indications, red flags, prehospital ABC and transfer, admission criteria, extradural haematoma above 30 cc and subdural haematoma above 10 mm with midline shift above 5 mm for surgery, PaCO2 30–35 mmHg, head-end elevation, mannitol 20% 200 mL (adults) only if systolic BP above 90 mmHg, mannitol 0.25–1 g/kg, 3% saline 3 mL/kg 8-hourly, phenytoin 20 mg/kg then 5 mg/kg/day, levetiracetam 500 mg twice daily for 1–3 months, steroids not useful, repeat CT at 24 hours checked against the ICMR Neurosurgery STW (July 2024).

Tranexamic acid 1 g over 10 minutes then 1 g over 8 hours within 3 hours for GCS 12 or less or intracranial bleed on CT checked against the CFPC CRASH-3 summary; BTF 4th edition BP, ICP, CPP, hyperventilation, steroid and seizure-prophylaxis statements from a Medical Dialogues summary.
unverifiedSections: The STW gives no SpO2 or blood-pressure target beyond systolic above 90 mmHg before mannitol.
The ICMR STW gives no tranexamic acid or analgesic doses; tranexamic acid is from the CRASH-3 summary (CFPC) and analgesia from the morphine label and a UK paediatric guideline.
BTF 4th edition targets were read in a secondary summary.
Anticoagulant reversal agents are named for referral only; no opened source gives a reversal regimen.
Intubation at GCS 8 or less is standard practice, not stated in the cited sources.
Children's mannitol dose is described as weight-based without a number; the 0.25–1 g/kg range is used.
The STW gives two PaCO2 ranges (30–35 and 30–32 mmHg); 30–35 mmHg is shown.
Drug cautions, contraindications and renal or hepatic adjustment lines without a source tag are general pharmacology statements and need formulary confirmation.

pathophysiology.summary: Traumatic brain injury (TBI) is a leading cause of death and disability among young people in India, mostly from road traffic crashes and falls. The primary injury happens at impact; much of the harm that follows is secondary injury from hypoxia, hypotension, raised intracranial pressure and seizures, which good early care prevents. The ICMR workflow asks for ABC stabilisation in the golden hour, a search for other injuries, GCS grading, early non-contrast CT with cervical spine imaging, admission for those at risk, osmotherapy for clinical signs of raised ICP once systolic BP is above 90 mmHg, and urgent neurosurgical referral for operable haematomas. Tranexamic acid given within 3 hours reduces head-injury death in patients with mild to moderate injury (CRASH-3), so timing of arrival matters as much as the scan.
keyMechanisms: Primary injury: contusion, diffuse axonal injury and haematomas at impact.
Secondary injury: hypoxia, hypotension, hypercarbia and seizures worsen brain damage.
Expanding haematoma or oedema raises ICP and reduces cerebral perfusion, leading to herniation.
Osmotic agents draw water out of the brain to lower ICP.

symptoms: Vomiting (persistent vomiting is a CT indication) (ICMR STW)
physicalSigns: Scalp wound, skull fracture, cerebrospinal fluid leak
redFlags: Unconscious; irregular respiration; asymmetric pupils (ICMR STW)
Falling GCS, new focal deficit (ICMR STW)
precipitants: Road traffic crashes, often without helmet

differentials.distinguishingFeatures: Often coexists with head injury; never let it explain a low GCS — CT the head and recheck GCS as levels fall.
Low capillary glucose that corrects with dextrose; check glucose in every patient with reduced consciousness.

differentials.condition: Stroke or intracranial haemorrhage causing the fall
differentials.distinguishingFeatures: Focal deficit out of proportion to trauma or sudden onset before the fall; CT and CT angiography settle it.
Witnessed seizure before the fall, tongue bite, gradual recovery of GCS; CT still needed if injury occurred.
Neck pain, tenderness or neurological deficit; immobilise and image the cervical spine with the head CT (ICMR STW).
History inconsistent with injuries, delayed presentation, multiple bruises of different ages; skeletal survey and safeguarding.

diagnosticCriteria.threshold: GCS below 15, transient loss of consciousness, suspected skull fracture, post-traumatic seizure, focal deficit, persistent vomiting, amnesia.
Extradural haematoma above 30 cc; subdural haematoma above 10 mm thick with midline shift above 5 mm and deterioration.
GCS 12 or less, or intracranial bleeding on CT, without major extracranial bleeding, within 3 hours of injury.
Systolic BP 100 mmHg or more (age 50–69) or 110 mmHg or more (15–49 or over 70); treat ICP above 22 mmHg; CPP 60–70 mmHg.

ruleIn.expectedFinding: Fall in GCS; unequal or unreactive pupils

clinicalManagement.title: Prehospital and arrival
actions: ABC per trauma guidelines; control external bleeding; immobilise the cervical spine (ICMR STW).
Transfer once ABC stable to a centre with CT and a neurosurgeon (ICMR STW).

clinicalManagement.title: Anticoagulants, antiplatelets and wounds
actions: Ask about warfarin, direct oral anticoagulants and antiplatelets; CT all anticoagulated patients and arrange urgent reversal with haematology if bleeding.
Clean and close scalp wounds; tetanus toxoid 0.5 mL IM if not already given (DGHS STG).

clinicalManagement.title: Assess and image
actions: GCS, pupils, focal signs; search for other injuries (ICMR STW).
Non-contrast CT head with cervical spine imaging (ICMR STW).

clinicalManagement.title: Raised ICP
actions: Elevate the head end; sedation and analgesia; PaCO2 30–35 mmHg if ventilated (ICMR STW).
Mannitol only if systolic BP above 90 mmHg and red flags; or 3% saline (ICMR STW).

clinicalManagement.title: Tranexamic acid and analgesia
actions: Tranexamic acid 1 g IV over 10 minutes then 1 g over 8 hours if GCS 12 or less or bleeding on CT, within 3 hours (CRASH-3).
Pain relief with paracetamol and titrated IV morphine; avoid oversedation that masks a falling GCS.

clinicalManagement.title: Severe TBI in the intensive care unit (ICU)
actions: Keep systolic BP 100–110 mmHg or more by age; treat ICP above 22 mmHg; CPP 60–70 mmHg (BTF).
Avoid prolonged hyperventilation to PaCO2 25 mmHg or less; no steroids (BTF).
Phenytoin for early seizures (first 7 days); start feeding by day 5–7 (BTF).

clinicalManagement.title: Surgery
actions: Extradural above 30 cc or subdural above 10 mm with shift above 5 mm and deterioration: neurosurgery (ICMR STW).
Decompressive craniectomy by a neurosurgeon only (ICMR STW).

clinicalManagement.title: Admit or discharge
actions: Admit: amnesia, loss of consciousness, falling consciousness, moderate–severe headache, intoxication, skull fracture, other injury or abnormal CT (ICMR STW).
Others: discharge with head-injury advice and return precautions (ICMR STW).

vignette.text: A 27-year-old motorcyclist without a helmet is brought to a district hospital in Bihar 90 minutes after colliding with a tractor. He was unconscious for about 2 minutes, has vomited twice and smells of alcohol. GCS is 12 (E3 V4 M5), pupils are equal and reactive, BP 132/84 mmHg, pulse 96/min and SpO2 97% on air. There is a boggy scalp swelling over the left temple. The nearest CT scanner is 70 km away.

guidedApproach.title: Primary and secondary brain injury
guidedApproach.prompt: Why does early care change outcome when the impact has already happened?
guidedApproach.guidance: The damage at impact — contusion, axonal shearing and haematoma — cannot be undone, but much of the disability after head injury comes from secondary injury in the hours that follow. Hypoxia, hypotension, hypercarbia, hypoglycaemia, seizures and an expanding haematoma all reduce oxygen delivery to brain tissue that is already vulnerable. A single episode of hypotension or hypoxia during transfer is associated with worse outcome. This is why the workflow insists on stabilising airway, breathing and circulation before transfer, and why a falling GCS, a widening pupil or the Cushing response (bradycardia with hypertension) are emergencies: they signal rising intracranial pressure and impending herniation. Tranexamic acid works on the same principle — it limits haematoma growth when given within 3 hours.

guidedApproach.title: Reading the GCS and the red flags
guidedApproach.prompt: How do you recognise the patient who is getting worse?
guidedApproach.guidance: Record the GCS by its components (eye, verbal, motor), because a change in motor score is the most reliable sign of deterioration. Mild injury is GCS 13–15, moderate 9–12 and severe 3–8. A drop of even one or two points, a new focal deficit, unequal pupils, persistent vomiting, worsening headache or restlessness all mean the brain is under threat. Alcohol is common in Indian road-traffic injuries and is a trap: an intoxicated patient with a low GCS must be scanned and reassessed, never assumed to be 'just drunk'. Always look for associated injuries to the chest, abdomen, pelvis and long bones, because blood loss elsewhere causes the hypotension that harms the brain.

guidedApproach.title: Who needs a CT and when
guidedApproach.prompt: Which patients need imaging, and what does the scan decide?
guidedApproach.guidance: Non-contrast CT of the head with cervical spine imaging is the key test and should be done as soon as possible in anyone who is not completely asymptomatic. The workflow lists definite indications: GCS below 15, any loss of consciousness, suspected skull fracture, post-traumatic seizure, a focal deficit, persistent vomiting or amnesia. The CT answers three questions: is there a lesion that needs surgery (an extradural haematoma above 30 cc, or a subdural above 10 mm with midline shift above 5 mm and deterioration); does the patient need admission; and is there bleeding that makes tranexamic acid worthwhile. Where the scanner is far away, stabilise first, give tranexamic acid if within 3 hours and GCS is 12 or less, and transfer with monitoring.

guidedApproach.title: Protecting the brain until definitive care
guidedApproach.prompt: What are the priorities for a moderate or severe head injury?
guidedApproach.guidance: Secure the airway (by standard practice, intubate if GCS is 8 or less or the airway is at risk), keep oxygen saturation and blood pressure normal — in severe injury, systolic BP of at least 100–110 mmHg depending on age — and elevate the head of the bed. Give tranexamic acid 1 g over 10 minutes then 1 g over 8 hours within 3 hours for GCS 12 or less or a bleed on CT. Signs of rising ICP with an adequate BP are treated with mannitol or 3% saline as a bridge to surgery; prolonged hyperventilation and steroids do not help. Phenytoin or levetiracetam is used for post-traumatic seizures. Treat pain with paracetamol and carefully titrated morphine, checking GCS and pupils before each opioid dose so that sedation does not hide deterioration.

boardQuestions.vignette: A 27-year-old man arrives 90 minutes after a motorcycle crash. He was unconscious for 2 minutes and has GCS 12 with equal pupils. BP is 132/84 mmHg and SpO2 97%. The nearest CT scanner is 70 km away, and there is no other bleeding.
boardQuestions.question: Which is the most appropriate step before transfer?

options.text: Give tranexamic acid 1 g IV over 10 minutes, then 1 g over 8 hours
options.explanation: Correct. GCS 12 within 3 hours of injury meets CRASH-3 criteria; the infusion can run during transfer.

options.text: Give dexamethasone to reduce brain swelling
options.explanation: Steroids do not improve outcome or lower ICP in head injury (ICMR STW; BTF).
Mannitol is for clinical signs of raised ICP with systolic BP above 90 mmHg; he has none.

options.text: Wait until the CT result before any treatment
options.explanation: Tranexamic acid only helps within 3 hours; waiting for a distant CT would lose the window.

options.text: Hyperventilate to a PaCO2 of 25 mmHg
options.explanation: Prolonged hyperventilation to 25 mmHg or less is not recommended (BTF).

boardQuestions.educationalObjective: Recognise the indication and time window for tranexamic acid in TBI.
boardQuestions.keyPoint: GCS 12 or less or bleed on CT, within 3 hours: tranexamic acid 1 g + 1 g.

boardQuestions.vignette: A 45-year-old woman fell from a ladder. GCS was 14 on arrival and is now 10 an hour later, with a dilating right pupil. BP 168/90 mmHg, pulse 54/min. CT shows a right extradural haematoma of 45 cc with midline shift.
boardQuestions.question: What is the best next step?

options.explanation: Observation alone is unsafe: she has a surgical lesion and signs of herniation.

options.text: Urgent neurosurgical evacuation, with mannitol as a bridge
options.explanation: Correct. An extradural haematoma above 30 cc needs surgery (ICMR STW); mannitol is appropriate with systolic BP above 90 mmHg and red flags.

options.text: Start phenytoin and repeat CT in 24 hours
options.explanation: Seizure prophylaxis does not treat an expanding haematoma; delay risks death.
Bradycardia with hypertension is the Cushing response to raised ICP; the treatment is decompression.
Lumbar puncture is dangerous with a mass lesion and raised ICP (risk of herniation).

boardQuestions.educationalObjective: Identify a surgical lesion and the signs of herniation.
boardQuestions.keyPoint: Extradural haematoma above 30 cc, or deterioration with shift: neurosurgery now.

boardQuestions.vignette: A 35-year-old man was assaulted and is drowsy, smells strongly of alcohol, and has GCS 13. He has a 4 cm scalp laceration over the occiput but no vomiting, and his pupils are equal. His friends say he is 'just drunk', that he often drinks this much, and want to take him home tonight.
boardQuestions.question: What is the most appropriate management?

options.text: Allow discharge with friends because the GCS is above 12
options.explanation: GCS below 15 after head injury is a CT indication (ICMR STW); alcohol does not explain it safely.

options.text: Observe until sober, then decide on imaging
options.explanation: Waiting delays the diagnosis of an intracranial bleed; intoxication is an admission criterion in itself.

options.text: CT head with cervical spine imaging and admission for observation
options.explanation: Correct. GCS below 15 mandates CT, and intoxication is an admission criterion (ICMR STW).
Naloxone has no role unless opioid toxicity is suspected; it does not exclude brain injury.
Skull X-ray does not show intracranial bleeding; CT is the test.

boardQuestions.educationalObjective: Do not attribute a low GCS to alcohol after head injury.
boardQuestions.keyPoint: Head injury + intoxication: CT and admit; never assume 'just drunk'.

patientEducation: Return at once for drowsiness, vomiting, severe headache, seizure, weakness or confusion.
dischargeCriteria: GCS 15, no red flags, CT normal or stable (ICMR STW)
nonClinicalManagement.followUpPlan: Review for persistent headache, memory or mood symptoms; antiseizure medicine review by neurosurgeon or neurologist (ICMR STW).
